name: Subcision / TCA CROSS

lead: Subcision uses a needle under the skin to release the bands that tether depressed acne scars, described in 1995. TCA CROSS is a separate acid-based scar procedure often mentioned alongside it.
Dermatology reviews treat subcision as one part of multimodality scar care, with studies mostly small case series and registered trials.

paras: Cutting the fibrous tether is described as letting the scar rise, with a wound-healing response adding collagen.
Grokipedia lists bleeding disorders, infection and keloid tendency as contraindications. Sources reviewed give limited complication data.

lead: Subcision is a minor surgical procedure for depressed (atrophic) scars in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin and moved to cut the fibrous bands that hold a scar down. It was named and described in 1995 by Orentreich and Orentreich as subcutaneous incisionless surgery for depressed scars and wrinkles [1]. TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a separate scar procedure that uses trichloroacetic acid; it is grouped with subcision in community discussion of scar treatment, but the sources reviewed for this article do not describe it in detail.

Subcision is mainly applied to rolling acne scars, which dermatologists classify as one of three atrophic scar types alongside icepick and boxcar scars [2][3]. It has also been studied for cellulite [4][5]. Reviews of acne-scar management describe it as one component of multimodality treatment tailored to scar type [6][7].

On looksmax.org, subcision is discussed as a step used when other treatments have not improved tethered scars, and the forum includes self-performed ('DIY') accounts. This article documents that the practice is discussed but does not describe how to perform it.
infobox: Minor in-office procedure (subcision); chemical scar procedure (TCA CROSS)
Limited to moderate (small studies, case series, reviews)

paras: In the original description, a tri-beveled hypodermic needle is introduced through a skin puncture, hence 'incisionless', and its sharp edges are moved under the defect to make cuts beneath the skin surface [1]. Per Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, the aim is to release fibrous attachments between a scar and deeper tissue so the skin can rise, and to trigger a wound-healing response [8]. Practitioner descriptions say this works best on tethered, rolling scars; Grokipedia lists bleeding disorders, active infection and a tendency to form keloids as contraindications [8].

A widely cited 2001 classification divides atrophic acne scars into icepick, boxcar and rolling types, with treatment choice depending on type [2]. A 2019 update reviewed newer and developing options within that system [3]. Reviews of multimodality care note that subcision is often combined with other treatments such as lasers, peels or microneedling [6][7]. A 2011 report described combined microneedling and glycolic acid peels for acne scars in dark skin, listing subcision among the options for scars [9].

A 2005 case series of 40 patients examined subcision technique and outcomes for acne scarring [10]. Subcision for cellulite has been the subject of a 2000 report and a 2017 review [4][5]. Laser treatments for facial acne scars have been separately reviewed [11].

Registered trials include subcision with CO2 laser or PRP versus subcision alone (42 participants, 2025) [12]; subcision with injected exosomes versus subcision alone (20 participants, 2024, completed) [13]; subcision with suction (20 participants, 2012, completed) [14]; multiple subcisions on rolling scars (5 participants, 2014) [15]; cannula versus needle subcision for post-traumatic atrophic facial scars (50 participants, 2021) [16]; and combination procedures for acne scarring (30 participants, 2007) [17]. Cellulite trials combining subcision with cryolipolysis are also registered [18]. The registry records reviewed list no outcomes.
A looksmax.org thread promotes subcision as a procedure that releases scars from underlying tissue and can be followed by lasers or peels [19].
